blocks.title: Free oscillations
blocks.text: A body executes free vibrations if it oscillates at its natural frequency without the interference of an external force.

For example, a simple pendulum slightly displaced from its mean position vibrates freely at its natural frequency, which depends only on its length (Fig 14.12, a pendulum swinging from A through B to C). In free oscillations, with no resistive force, the total energy of the body stays constant and so the amplitude stays constant.

blocks.title: Forced oscillations
blocks.text: If a freely oscillating system is acted on by an external periodic force, forced vibrations take place, for example when a swing is pushed repeatedly (Fig 14.13).

The vibrations of a factory floor caused by heavy machinery are an example of forced vibrations. Another example is the loud sound produced by the wooden boards of string instruments, which are made to vibrate by the strings. The book's Figs 14.12 and 14.13 (a pendulum and a child being pushed on a swing) are drawings described here.

blocks.title: Interesting information
blocks.text: A guitar string, a ringing bell, atomic oscillations, bridge vibrations and the sway of a building are given in the book as examples of free oscillations.

blocks.prompt: Is a child on a swing who is pushed once and then left alone doing free or forced oscillation? What if the child is pushed every cycle?
blocks.explanation: Pushed once and left: free oscillation (at the swing's natural frequency, slowly dying away). Pushed every cycle: forced oscillation.

items: Free oscillation: at the natural frequency, no external force.
Forced oscillation: driven by an external periodic force (pushed swing, factory floor).
